title: REST API Design
description: Learn how to design clean, predictable REST APIs with proper resources, CRUD mapping, pagination, versioning, and HATEOAS.

segments.text: APIs are how software talks to software. REST is the most popular style for web APIs. But most developers misunderstand it. Let's see what makes a truly RESTful API and why good design matters.

REST is all about resources. A resource is any noun in your system — users, orders, products. Each resource gets a unique URL. Slash users slash forty-two identifies user forty-two. Keep URLs noun-based, never verb-based.
HTTP methods map to CRUD operations. GET reads. POST creates. PUT replaces. PATCH updates partially. DELETE removes. The URL stays the same — only the method changes. That's the beauty of REST.
Here's a common mistake. Developers create URLs like slash get-user or slash delete-order. That's putting verbs in URLs. REST already has verbs — they're the HTTP methods.

When a resource has thousands of items, you can't return them all at once. Pagination solves this. Offset-based uses page and limit parameters. Cursor-based uses an opaque token pointing to the next batch. Cursors are better for real-time data.

Filtering lets clients ask for exactly what they need. Query parameters work well — slash users question mark status equals active ampersand role equals admin. Keep filters predictable and documented. Avoid inventing custom query languages.

APIs evolve, but clients depend on existing behavior. Versioning prevents breaking changes. URL versioning uses slash v1 slash users. Header versioning uses Accept headers. URL versioning is simpler and more widely adopted.

Use proper status codes. Two-oh-one for created resources. Two-oh-four for successful deletes with no body. Four-twenty-two for validation errors. Consistent error responses with a code, message, and details field make debugging painless.

HATEOAS takes REST further. Each response includes links to related actions — 'here's the order, and here are links to cancel it, update it, or view its items.' The API becomes self-discoverable. Clients don't need to hardcode URLs.
In practice, very few APIs implement HATEOAS fully. Most settle for 'pragmatic REST' — good URLs, proper methods, clear status codes. And honestly, that's usually enough.
segments.thought_prompt: What benefits does HATEOAS provide that make the extra complexity worthwhile?

segments.text: Good REST API design is about clarity and consistency. Noun-based URLs, proper HTTP methods, pagination, filtering, versioning, and meaningful status codes. Get these right and your API will be a joy to use. Next, we'll tackle authentication.
